cards.q: Consider min f(x) over a set S ⊆ ℝⁿ, and let B(x*, ε) be the ball of radius ε around x*. Define (1) a global minimizer, (2) a local minimizer, (3) the strict version of each. (4) How do these notions imply one another?
pts: (1) Global: f(x) ≥ f(x*) for all x ∈ S.
(2) Local: there is ε > 0 with f(x) ≥ f(x*) for all x ∈ B(x*, ε) ∩ S.
(3) Strict: replace ≥ with > for every x ≠ x* (in S, or in the ball).
(4) Strict global ⇒ global ⇒ local, and strict global ⇒ strict local ⇒ local. A strict global minimizer is unique.
cards.pit: Global does not imply strict: for a constant function every point is a global min and none is strict.

cards.q: Let b ∈ ℝⁿ, and let B be an n×n matrix that is not necessarily symmetric. Gradients are column vectors. Give the gradient and Hessian of (1) bᵀx, (2) xᵀBx, (3) f(x) = ½xᵀAx + bᵀx + c where A is symmetric.
pts: (1) Gradient b, Hessian 0.
(2) Gradient (B + Bᵀ)x, Hessian B + Bᵀ.
(3) Gradient Ax + b, Hessian A.
cards.pit: ∇(xᵀBx) = 2Bx only when B is symmetric. The slide's derivative table drops this condition.

cards.q: Consider the unconstrained problem min f(x) over x ∈ ℝⁿ. State the first-order necessary condition (FONC): (1) what is assumed about f and about the point x*, (2) what is concluded, (3) is the converse true?
pts: (1) f is differentiable at x*, and x* is a local minimizer over ℝⁿ.
(2) ∇f(x*) = 0. A point with zero gradient is called a stationary point.
(3) No. f(x) = x³ has f′(0) = 0, but 0 is neither a min nor a max.
cards.pit: FONC is only a filter: it removes non-stationary points, it never certifies a minimizer by itself.

cards.q: FONC: if x* is a local minimizer of a differentiable f on ℝⁿ, then ∇f(x*) = 0. Outline a rigorous proof. (1) What inequality do you start from? (2) How do you turn it into a statement about ∇f(x*)ᵀd? (3) How do you conclude ∇f(x*) = 0?
pts: (1) Fix any direction d. For small t > 0 the point x* + td is inside the ball of local optimality, so f(x* + td) − f(x*) ≥ 0.
(2) Divide by t > 0 and let t ↓ 0. By first-order Taylor, f(x* + td) − f(x*) = t∇f(x*)ᵀd + o(t), so ∇f(x*)ᵀd ≥ 0 for every d.
(3) Choose d = −∇f(x*). This gives −‖∇f(x*)‖² ≥ 0, so ∇f(x*) = 0.
cards.pit: The slide ends with “∇f(x*)ᵀd = 0 and d ≠ 0, so ∇f(x*) = 0”. That is false for a single d (g = (1,0), d = (0,1)). The inequality must hold for all d.

cards.q: FONC reduces min f(x) over ℝⁿ to finding points with ∇f(x) = 0. (1) What does this achieve? (2) What three things can it not do? Give an example for each.
pts: (1) It rules out every non-stationary point, leaving a square system ∇f(x) = 0 (n equations, n unknowns).
(2a) It cannot tell a min from a max: f and −f have the same stationary points (x³ − x² − 4x − 6 has one of each).
(2b) It cannot rule out saddle points.
(2c) It may find nothing: f(x) = x₁ − 2x₂ has ∇f = (1, −2) ≠ 0 everywhere, and the problem is unbounded below.
cards.pit: Existence is a separate question. eˣ is strictly convex with infimum 0, yet has no minimizer and no stationary point.

cards.q: FONC assumes x* is an interior point and f is differentiable there. Explain what goes wrong in (1) minimizing f(x) = x over x ∈ [0, 1], whose minimizer is x* = 0, and (2) minimizing f(x) = |x|, whose minimizer is x* = 0.
pts: (1) x* = 0 is a boundary point, so only directions d ≥ 0 are feasible. The proof then gives ∇f(x*)ᵀd ≥ 0 only for feasible d, not ∇f(x*) = 0. Here f′(0) = 1 ≠ 0. This “no feasible descent direction” condition is the seed of KKT.
(2) |x| is not differentiable at 0 (one-sided derivatives are −1 and +1), so the hypothesis of FONC fails.
cards.pit: Non-smooth losses such as the hinge loss have the same issue at the kink. That is why subgradients exist.

cards.q: (1) Define a convex set C ⊆ ℝⁿ. (2) Name four standard examples. (3) An affine set {x : Ax = b} is convex. What stronger property does it have?
pts: (1) For all x, y ∈ C and λ ∈ [0, 1], the point λx + (1 − λ)y is in C: the segment between two points of C stays in C.
(2) Any four of: ℝⁿ, the empty set, half-spaces {aᵀx ≥ β}, balls, affine sets, the cone of PSD matrices.
(3) It contains the whole line through any two of its points: λx + (1 − λ)y is in the set for every real λ, not only λ ∈ [0, 1].
cards.pit: A union of convex sets is generally not convex: [0, 1] ∪ [2, 3] misses the midpoint 1.5.

cards.q: (1) Which three operations on convex sets give a convex set again? (2) Let g be a convex function. Why is {x : g(x) ≤ 0} convex? (3) Why is the LP feasible set {x : Ax ≤ b} convex?
pts: (1) Intersection (of any number of sets), scaling βC, and the Minkowski sum C₁ + C₂.
(2) If g(x) ≤ 0 and g(y) ≤ 0, then g(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λg(x) + (1 − λ)g(y) ≤ 0.
(3) Each row aᵢᵀx ≤ bᵢ is a half-space, and the set is the intersection of these half-spaces.
cards.pit: Unions do not preserve convexity.

cards.q: Let f be a real-valued function on a set S ⊆ ℝⁿ. (1) Define “f is convex” and give the geometric picture. (2) Define “strictly convex” and “concave”. (3) Why must S be a convex set?
pts: (1) f(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≤ λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y) for all x, y ∈ S and λ ∈ [0, 1]. The chord between two points of the graph lies on or above the graph.
(2) Strictly convex: the inequality is strict whenever x ≠ y and λ ∈ (0, 1). Concave: −f is convex.
(3) The definition evaluates f at λx + (1 − λ)y, so that point has to lie in S.
cards.pit: “Is 1/x convex?” is ill-posed on ℝ∖{0}, which is not a convex set. On (0, ∞) it is convex.

cards.q: Let f(x) = ½xᵀAx + bᵀx + c with A symmetric. (1) When is f convex, and when strictly convex? (2) Which identity proves this directly from the definition of convexity? (3) Apply the result to portfolio variance xᵀQx, where Q is the covariance matrix of asset returns r and x the weights.
pts: (1) Convex ⇔ A ⪰ 0 (PSD). Strictly convex ⇔ A ≻ 0 (PD).
(2) λf(x) + (1 − λ)f(y) − f(λx + (1 − λ)y) = ½λ(1 − λ)(x − y)ᵀA(x − y). The gap is ≥ 0 for all x, y exactly when A ⪰ 0.
(3) xᵀQx = Var(xᵀr) ≥ 0, so Q is PSD and variance is convex in x. It is strictly convex iff Q ≻ 0, i.e. no combination of the assets is riskless.
cards.pit: The condition is also necessary: if vᵀAv < 0 for some v, take x − y = v and the gap becomes negative.

cards.q: Let f, f₁, f₂ be convex functions on a convex set. Under what conditions are the following convex: (1) f₁ + f₂ and αf, (2) the composition g(f(x)) with g: ℝ → ℝ, (3) f(Ax + b) and max{f₁(x), f₂(x)}?
pts: (1) f₁ + f₂ always (strictly convex if one of them is). αf when α > 0.
(2) When g is convex and nondecreasing on the range of f.
(3) Both always. These two rules are not on the slides, but they are what makes the hinge loss (a max of affine functions) and the logistic loss (a convex function of an affine map) convex.
cards.pit: Rule (2) needs “nondecreasing”: g(y) = e^(−y) is convex and x² is convex, but e^(−x²) has second derivative −2 at 0.

cards.q: Let H(x) be the Hessian of f. State the Hessian test for convexity of f on a set C: (1) what is assumed about C and f, (2) the test for convexity, (3) the test for strict convexity, and whether it works in both directions.
pts: (1) C is non-empty, open and convex, and f is twice continuously differentiable on C.
(2) f is convex on C ⇔ H(x) ⪰ 0 at every x ∈ C.
(3) H(x) ≻ 0 at every x ∈ C ⇒ f is strictly convex. One direction only: x⁴ is strictly convex, yet its second derivative is 0 at x = 0.
cards.pit: The slide says “strictly convex iff PD”, which is wrong in the ⇒ direction. Also, H ⪰ 0 at one point proves nothing: it must hold on all of C.

cards.q: Let A be a symmetric matrix. How do you check (1) that A is positive definite (PD), (2) that A is positive semidefinite (PSD)? (3) Write the PSD conditions for the 2×2 matrix with rows (a, b) and (b, c).
pts: (1) All leading principal minors > 0 (determinants of the upper-left k×k blocks), or all eigenvalues > 0.
(2) All principal minors ≥ 0, not only the leading ones, or all eigenvalues ≥ 0.
(3) a ≥ 0, c ≥ 0 and ac − b² ≥ 0.
cards.pit: Leading minors ≥ 0 does not give PSD: diag(0, −1) has leading minors 0 and 0, but it is not PSD.

cards.q: A convex problem is min f(x) over x ∈ S where S is a convex set and f is convex on S. (1) State the “local = global” theorem, including what strict convexity adds. (2) Outline the proof: x* is a local minimizer with radius ε and y ∈ S is any point outside the ball B(x*, ε). Which point z do you construct, and how do you finish?
pts: (1) Every local minimizer is a global minimizer. If f is strictly convex, the minimizer is also unique (and strict).

(2) Take z = λ′x* + (1 − λ′)y with 1 − λ′ = ε/‖y − x*‖. Then z ∈ S because S is convex, and z lies on the ball. So f(x*) ≤ f(z) ≤ λ′f(x*) + (1 − λ′)f(y), using local optimality then convexity of f. Divide by 1 − λ′ > 0 to get f(x*) ≤ f(y).
cards.pit: Both convexities are needed. (x − 2)² on S = [−1, 0] ∪ [1, 3] has a local min at 0 that is not global, because S is not convex.

cards.q: Let f be differentiable on an open convex set C. (1) State the gradient inequality that is equivalent to convexity of f, and give its geometric meaning. (2) Suppose f is convex and ∇f(x*) = 0. What follows, and why? (3) What does this mean for FONC when f is convex on ℝⁿ?
pts: (1) f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x) for all x, y ∈ C. The tangent plane at any point lies below the graph everywhere.
(2) x* is a global minimizer: put x = x* in the inequality to get f(y) ≥ f(x*) for all y.
(3) FONC becomes necessary and sufficient: x* is a global minimizer ⇔ ∇f(x*) = 0.
cards.pit: On a constrained convex set S the minimizer need not be stationary. The right condition is ∇f(x*)ᵀ(y − x*) ≥ 0 for all y ∈ S.

cards.q: Least squares: X is the data matrix (n samples × d features), y ∈ ℝⁿ the targets, and we choose weights w ∈ ℝᵈ to minimize f(w) = ½‖Xw − y‖². (1) Give ∇f and the Hessian, and explain why f is always convex. (2) When is the minimizer unique, and what is it? (3) What does the optimality condition say about the residual r = Xw* − y? (4) What happens when the uniqueness condition fails?
pts: (1) ∇f(w) = Xᵀ(Xw − y), Hessian XᵀX. The Hessian is PSD because wᵀXᵀXw = ‖Xw‖² ≥ 0, so f is convex for any X.
(2) Unique iff X has full column rank (no redundant features). Then XᵀX is PD, and ∇f = 0 gives w* = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy.
(3) Xᵀr = 0: the residual is orthogonal to every column of X.
(4) XᵀX is singular. f is still convex, so every local min is global, but there are infinitely many minimizers. Ridge (XᵀX + γI) restores uniqueness.
cards.pit: The slides say “full row rank”, which is backwards. A tall regression matrix (n > d) can never have full row rank. What is needed is full column rank.

cards.q: Let f be twice differentiable on ℝⁿ with Hessian H(x), and suppose f is not known to be convex. State (1) the second-order necessary condition (SONC), (2) the second-order sufficient condition (SOSC). (3) Which case can neither condition decide? Give examples.
pts: (1) SONC: if x* is a local min, then ∇f(x*) = 0 and H(x*) ⪰ 0.
(2) SOSC: if ∇f(x*) = 0 and H(x*) ≻ 0, then x* is a strict local min.
(3) ∇f(x*) = 0 with H(x*) PSD but singular. x⁴ has a minimum at 0 while x³ has neither a min nor a max there, and both have second derivative 0.
cards.pit: SOSC is local only. x³ − x² − 4x − 6 has a strict local min, yet it is unbounded below. A global conclusion needs H ⪰ 0 everywhere (convexity).

cards.q: Let x* be a stationary point of f, i.e. ∇f(x*) = 0. (1) What does it mean for x* to be a saddle point? (2) Which condition on the Hessian H(x*) guarantees a saddle point, and how do you check it?
pts: (1) x* is neither a local min nor a local max: every neighbourhood contains points with f larger and points with f smaller than f(x*).
(2) H(x*) is indefinite, i.e. it has at least one positive and at least one negative eigenvalue.
cards.pit: Indefinite is sufficient, not necessary. x₁² − x₂⁴ has H(0) = diag(2, 0), which is PSD, yet 0 is a saddle. x₁² + x₂⁴ has the same Hessian and a strict min.

cards.q: Let f(x) = x³ − x² − 4x − 6 on ℝ. (1) Find the stationary points. (2) Classify each with the second derivative. (3) Does f have a global minimum?
pts: (2) f″(x) = 6x − 2. At (1 + √13)/3 it equals 2√13 > 0: strict local min. At (1 − √13)/3 it equals −2√13 < 0: strict local max.
cards.pit: The slide prints the derivative as 3x² − 2x − 2, which does not match the stationary points it quotes. The correct one is 3x² − 2x − 4.

cards.q: For each function, say whether it is convex on the stated domain and give a one-line reason: (1) e^(ax) on ℝ, (2) −log x on (0, ∞), (3) the hinge loss max(0, 1 − z) on ℝ, (4) e^(−x²) on ℝ.
pts: (1) Convex: second derivative a²e^(ax) ≥ 0.
(2) Convex (strictly): second derivative 1/x² > 0.
(3) Convex: it is the maximum of two affine functions, 0 and 1 − z.
(4) Not convex: the second derivative is (4x² − 2)e^(−x²), which is −2 at x = 0.
cards.pit: The hinge loss is convex but not differentiable at z = 1, and not strictly convex (it is piecewise linear).
